t.3.59.1: Just as your father's kingdom is yours, so too is it mine, there is no doubt. But I will by no means go there while I am in misfortune.
t.3.59.2: Having once gone there prosperous, adding to your joy, how shall I now go there wretched, adding to your grief?
t.3.59.3: Speaking thus again and again, King Nala comforted the lovely Damayantī, who was covered with half of a single garment.
t.3.59.5: Then, having reached that hall, the king, lord of the Niṣadhas, together with Vaidarbhī, sat down upon the ground.
t.3.59.4: The two of them, wrapped in a single garment and wandering here and there, exhausted by hunger and thirst, came upon a certain shelter.
t.3.59.6: He, without clothing, dirty, with dishevelled hair and covered in dust, weary, slept on the bare ground together with Damayantī.
t.3.59.7: And Damayantī too, the lovely one, delicate and pitiable, having suddenly met with sorrow, was then carried away by sleep.
t.3.59.8: But while Damayantī slept, O lord of the people, King Nala, his mind and heart churned up by grief, did not sleep as he had before.
t.3.59.9: Seeing the seizure of his kingdom, his utter desertion by his friends, and that ruin of his in the forest, he fell into anxious brooding.
t.3.59.11: Devoted to me as she is, she suffers this misery for my sake; but without me, she might perhaps go back to her own people.
t.3.59.10: What would become of me if I did this, and what would become of me if I did not? Is death better for me, or the abandoning of this person?
t.3.59.12: With me, this peerless woman will without doubt meet with sorrow; but if I abandon her, there would be uncertainty, and she might perhaps find happiness somewhere.
t.3.59.13: Having deliberated in many ways and reflected again and again, that lord of men concluded that abandoning Damayantī would be for the best.
t.3.59.14: Reflecting on his own lack of clothing and on her having only a single garment, the king resolved upon cutting off half of the garment.
t.3.59.16: Then Nala, running about hither and thither, O Bhārata, came upon an excellent sword, unsheathed, in the vicinity of the hall.
t.3.59.15: "How can I cut the garment so that this beloved of mine does not wake?" Thinking thus, the Naiṣadha king then paced about the hall.
t.3.59.17: With it the scorcher of foes cut off half of the garment and wrapped himself in it, and, abandoning the sleeping Vaidarbhī, he ran away, bereft of his senses.
t.3.59.18: Then, his heart bound to her, the lord of the Niṣadhas came back again to that hall, and seeing Damayantī in that state, he wept.
t.3.59.19: My beloved, whom formerly neither the wind nor the sun beheld, she today lies on the ground in the midst of the assembly hall like one who has no protector.
t.3.59.20: This sweet-smiling woman of lovely hips, wrapped in a torn-off piece of cloth like a madwoman, how will she fare when she wakes and understands?
t.3.59.21: How will the lovely Bhaimī, a virtuous wife, separated from me and all alone, wander in this dreadful forest frequented by wild beasts and serpents?
t.3.59.22: Going away again and again, King Nala kept returning to the hall; dragged onward by Kali, he was drawn back by his love.
t.3.59.23: Then the heart of that grieving man was split as if in two; like a swing, he kept coming back and going again to the hall, over and over.
t.3.59.24: But Nala, dragged away by Kali and bewildered, fled, abandoning his sleeping wife after lamenting much and piteously.
t.3.59.25: His mind lost, touched by Kali, the king, pondering this and that, went away all the same, grief-stricken, abandoning his wife in the empty forest.
